claims.claim: The norepinephrine concentration in iBAT was tended to increase transiently after 24 hr of cast immobilization.
claims.source: We first focused on the sympathetic nervous system, a general inducer of BAT thermogenesis, (Bartness et al., 2010) and found that the norepinephrine concentration in iBAT was tended to increase transiently after 24 hr of cast immobilization (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurement data of norepinephrine concentration in iBAT and citation to prior work on sympathetic regulation.

claims.claim: Expression of Ucp1 mRNA in iBAT was significantly attenuated by sympathetic denervation in mice with or without subsequent cast immobilization.
claims.source: Expression of Ucp1 mRNA in iBAT was significantly attenuated by such denervation in mice with or without subsequent cast immobilization (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data comparing sham-operated and denervated mice.

claims.claim: Mice with denervated iBAT manifested a lower core body temperature compared with sham-operated mice after cold exposure at 4 °C for 1 hr, and cast immobilization further increased the extent of hypothermia in the denervated mice.
claims.source: Moreover, mice with denervated iBAT manifested a lower core body temperature compared with sham-operated mice after cold exposure at 4 °C for 1 hr, and cast immobilization further increased the extent of hypothermia in the denervated mice (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements in denervated versus sham-operated mice.

claims.claim: BAT thermogenesis is activated via sympathetic nerves to maintain core body temperature in cast-immobilized mice.
claims.source: These results suggested that BAT thermogenesis is activated via sympathetic nerves to maintain core body temperature in cast-immobilized mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the denervation experiments showing reduced thermogenesis when sympathetic innervation is disrupted.

claims.claim: Metabolomics analysis revealed increases in the amounts of carbohydrate metabolites and amino acids in iBAT that were apparent as early as 10 hr after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings, metabolomics analysis revealed increases in the amounts of carbohydrate metabolites and amino acids in iBAT that were apparent as early as 10 hr after cast immobilization, and several glucose and amino acid metabolic pathways were significantly activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data showing increased metabolite levels and citation to previous findings.

claims.claim: Increases in metabolites after cast immobilization were not apparent in mice with iBAT denervation.
claims.source: Increases in these metabolites after cast immobilization were not apparent in mice with iBAT denervation (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing denervated and sham-operated mice.

claims.claim: Expression of the genes for fatty acid and succinate transporters in iBAT was induced by cast immobilization and such induction was prevented by iBAT denervation.
claims.source: We found that expression of the genes for fatty acid (Figure 2C) and succinate (Figure 2D) transporters in iBAT was induced by cast immobilization and that such induction was prevented by iBAT denervation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data showing transporter upregulation that is dependent on innervation.

claims.claim: The concentration of succinate was increased in iBAT of cast-immobilized mice in a manner sensitive to iBAT denervation.
claims.source: The concentration of succinate was also increased in iBAT of cast-immobilized mice in a manner sensitive to iBAT denervation (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite measurement data comparing denervated and sham-operated mice.

claims.claim: Oxygen consumption and systemic lipid utilization were increased by cast immobilization in intact mice but not in those subjected to iBAT denervation.
claims.source: Consistent with these changes in metabolite levels, oxygen consumption and systemic lipid utilization were increased by cast immobilization in intact mice (Figure 2F and G) but not in those subjected to iBAT denervation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic measurements comparing intact and denervated mice.

claims.claim: The weight of epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) and hepatic glycogen content were reduced by cast immobilization.
claims.source: The weight of epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) and hepatic glycogen content were reduced by cast immobilization (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by tissue weight and glycogen measurement data.

claims.claim: Expression of the genes for glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase) and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) in the liver increased gradually after cast immobilization, peaking at day 5.
claims.source: Expression of the genes for glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase) and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) in the liver increased gradually after cast immobilization, peaking at day 5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting that gluconeogenesis was slowly activated in the cast-immobilized mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data showing temporal changes in gluconeogenic enzyme expression.

claims.claim: The amounts of free amino acids were increased in both soleus and extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles of cast-immobilized mice.
claims.source: The amounts of free amino acids were also increased in both soleus and extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles of cast-immobilized mice (Figure 3A), whereas those in serum and the liver were not increased by cast immobilization (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data showing amino acid concentrations in different tissues.

claims.claim: Gene expression for the ubiquitin ligases Atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 was increased during the early phase (days 1–3) of cast immobilization.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings (Kawanishi et al., 2018), we found that gene expression for the ubiquitin ligases Atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 was increased during the early phase (days 1–3) of cast immobilization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Expression of the genes for SLC1A5 and SLC38A2 was significantly increased in iBAT after cast immobilization for 10 hr.
claims.source: Expression of the genes for SLC1A5 (a sodium-dependent glutamate transporter) and SLC38A2 (a sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter) was significantly increased in iBAT after cast immobilization for 10 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data showing transporter upregulation in BAT.

claims.claim: Expression of the gene for SLC38A2 and BCKDHA was significantly increased in the liver by cast immobilization.
claims.source: In the liver, expression of the gene for SLC38A2, which is upregulated by extracellular amino acid deprivation, (Gazzola et al., 2001; Gjymishka et al., 2008) and of that for BCKDHA, which is thought to be upregulated under fasting conditions to oxidize BCAAs for gluconeogenesis, (Huang and Chuang, 1999; Kobayashi et al., 1999) was significantly increased by cast immobilization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to previous work on transporter regulation.

claims.claim: Gene expression for amino acid transporters (SLC1A5, SLC7A5, SLC38A2) and BCAAs catabolic enzymes (BCAT2, BCKDHA) in soleus was significantly decreased after cast immobilization.
claims.source: On the other hand, gene expression for amino acid transporters (SLC1A5, SLC7A5, SLC38A2) and BCAAs catabolic enzymes (BCAT2, BCKDHA) in soleus was significantly decreased after cast immobilization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N-S).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data showing downregulation in muscle.

claims.claim: Expression of the gene for SLC43A1 was significantly increased in soleus by cast immobilization.
claims.source: Expression of the gene for SLC43A1, which is upregulated by food deprivation and is thought to transport amino acids from cells to the external environment (Fukuhara et al., 2007), was significantly increased in soleus by cast immobilization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to previous work on transporter function.

claims.claim: Incorporation of [3H] leucine was significantly increased in iBAT, liver, and kidney of mice subjected to cast immobilization for 1 day.
claims.source: Incorporation of [3H] leucine was not increased in skeletal muscle of mice subjected to cast immobilization for 1 or 3 days (data not shown), whereas it was significantly increased in iBAT, liver, and kidney of those subjected to cast immobilization for 1 day (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by radiotracer uptake data showing differential leucine incorporation across tissues.

claims.claim: Gene expression for SLC25A44 was increased in iBAT at 24 hr after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Gene expression for SLC25A44, a mitochondrial BCAAs transporter that contributes to BAT thermogenesis (Yoneshiro et al., 2019), was increased in iBAT at 24 hr after cast immobilization (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to previous work on the transporter's role.

claims.claim: The early increases in expression of the genes for SLC25A44, SLC1A5, and SLC38A2 induced by cast immobilization in iBAT of intact mice were prevented by denervation of iBAT.
claims.source: However, the early increases in expression of the genes for SLC25A44, SLC1A5, and SLC38A2 induced by cast immobilization in iBAT of intact mice were prevented by denervation of iBAT (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data comparing denervated and sham-operated mice.

claims.claim: Free amino acids are utilized as an energy substrate in BAT and the liver rather than in skeletal muscle of cast-immobilized mice.
claims.source: Our results thus suggested that free amino acids are utilized as an energy substrate in BAT and the liver rather than in skeletal muscle of cast-immobilized mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the leucine uptake and gene expression data.

claims.claim: The IL-6 gene tended to be induced earlier and to a greater extent in iBAT and soleus than were genes for other cytokines.
claims.source: Gene expression analysis revealed that the IL-6 gene tended to be induced earlier and to a greater extent in iBAT and soleus than were genes for other cytokines including tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein–1 (MCP-1), IL-1β, IL-10, and IL-15; for batokines including fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and bone morphogenetic protein 8B (BMP8B); or for myokines including FGF21 and irisin (Figure 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression data across multiple cytokines and tissues.

claims.claim: The increase in the amount of Il6 mRNA was apparent as early as 6–10 hr in iBAT, whereas that in soleus was more gradual.
claims.source: Whereas the increase in the amount of Il6 mRNA was apparent as early as 6–10 hr in iBAT, that in soleus was more gradual (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by temporal gene expression data comparing BAT and muscle.

claims.claim: Expression of the genes for serum amyloid A3 (Saa3) and suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (Socs3) was increased in iBAT and soleus at the same time as was that of Il6.
claims.source: Expression of the genes for serum amyloid A3 (Saa3) and suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (Socs3), both of which are regulated by IL-6 signaling, was also increased in iBAT and soleus at the same time as was that of Il6 (Figure 4E–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data showing coordinated upregulation of IL-6 target genes.

claims.claim: Expression of Il6 was not induced by cast immobilization in denervated iBAT.
claims.source: However, expression of Il6 was not induced by cast immobilization in denervated iBAT (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data comparing denervated and sham-operated mice.

claims.claim: The serum concentration of IL-6 was significantly increased from 10 hr after cast immobilization.
claims.source: The serum concentration of IL-6 was significantly increased from 10 hr after cast immobilization (Figure 4N), whereas that of TNF-α was not altered in cast-immobilized mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1R).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data measuring serum IL-6 levels.

claims.claim: Cast immobilization induces Il6 expression in iBAT and skeletal muscle, and induction of Il6 expression by cast immobilization in iBAT is dependent on the sympathetic nervous system.
claims.source: Together, these results suggested that cast immobilization induces Il6 expression in iBAT and skeletal muscle, and that induction of Il6 expression by cast immobilization in iBAT is dependent on the sympathetic nervous system.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the denervation and gene expression data.

claims.claim: Expression of Ucp1 in iBAT was significantly increased at 24 hr after cast immobilization in both WT and IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: Expression of Ucp1 in iBAT was significantly increased at 24 hr after cast immobilization in both WT and IL-6 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: The core body temperature of cast-immobilized IL-6 KO mice was decreased to a greater extent by cold exposure at 4 °C for 4 hr compared with that of cast-immobilized WT mice.
claims.source: However, the core body temperature of cast-immobilized IL-6 KO mice was decreased to a greater extent by cold exposure at 4 °C for 4 hr compared with that of cast-immobilized WT mice (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Oxygen consumption was not increased in IL-6 KO mice after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Furthermore, unlike that in WT mice, oxygen consumption was not increased in IL-6 KO mice after cast immobilization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic measurements comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: The amounts of carbohydrate metabolites in iBAT were higher for IL-6 KO mice than for WT mice and were not increased substantially by cast immobilization in the mutant mice.
claims.source: Metabolomics analysis revealed that the amounts of carbohydrate metabolites, including glucose 1-phosphate, glucose 6-phosphate, and phosphoenolpyruvic acid, in iBAT were higher for IL-6 KO mice than for WT mice and were not increased substantially by cast immobilization in the mutant mice (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: The concentrations of amino acids in iBAT of WT mice were increased markedly at 24 hr after cast immobilization, but not in IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: Whereas the concentrations of amino acids such as Ser, Asn, Lys, Met, His, Phe, and Tyr in iBAT of WT mice were increased markedly at 24 hr after cast immobilization, such was not the case for IL-6 KO mice (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Expression of the genes for SLC25A44 and CD36 in iBAT of IL-6 KO mice was not increased further at 24 hr after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Expression of the genes for SLC25A44, BCKDHA, and CD36 in iBAT was higher for IL-6 KO mice than for WT mice, but expression of the genes for SLC25A44 and CD36 in iBAT of IL-6 KO mice was not increased further at 24 hr after cast immobilization (Figure 5D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Incorporation of [3H] leucine was not increased in iBAT of IL-6 KO mice after cast immobilization for 24 hr.
claims.source: Incorporation of [3H] leucine was also not increased in iBAT of IL-6 KO mice after cast immobilization for 24 hr (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by radiotracer uptake data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Cast immobilization did not result in a loss of eWAT mass in IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: We found that, unlike in WT mice, cast immobilization did not result in a loss of eWAT mass in IL-6 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by tissue weight measurements comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Deficiency of IL-6 impairs the maintenance of core body temperature and alters energy metabolism in BAT and skeletal muscle in mice subjected to cast immobilization.
claims.source: These findings suggested that deficiency of IL-6 impairs the maintenance of core body temperature and alters energy metabolism in BAT and skeletal muscle in mice subjected to cast immobilization.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the collective data from IL-6 KO mice experiments.

claims.claim: The amounts of BCAAs in soleus were significantly increased after cast immobilization in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: The amounts of BCAAs in soleus were significantly increased after cast immobilization in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice (Figure 5H-J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice.

claims.claim: Administration of IL-6 restored the increase in the amounts of amino acids, including BCAAs in soleus of IL-6 KO mice with cast immobilization.
claims.source: Administration of IL-6 restored the increase in the amounts of amino acids, including BCAAs in soleus of IL-6 KO mice with cast immobilization (Figure 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from IL-6 administration experiments.

claims.claim: Treatment with IL-6 increased expression of Saa3 and Socs3 as well as the amounts of BCAAs in cultured mouse C2C12 myotubes.
claims.source: Treatment with IL-6 also increased expression of Saa3 and Socs3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) as well as the amounts of BCAAs (Figure 6D) in cultured mouse C2C12 myotubes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cell culture data showing IL-6 effects on myotubes.

claims.claim: Core body temperature of cold-exposed mice with cast immobilization and denervated iBAT was not significantly increased by administration of IL-6.
claims.source: We, therefore, examined whether IL-6 might increase core body temperature via the sympathetic nervous system with the use of C57BL/6 J mice with denervated iBAT. Core body temperature of cold-exposed mice with cast immobilization and denervated iBAT was not significantly increased by administration of IL-6 (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements in denervated mice treated with IL-6.

claims.claim: The serum IL-6 concentration of mice depleted of iBAT was not increased after cast immobilization.
claims.source: We first focused on the acute expression of the IL-6 gene apparent in iBAT after cast immobilization (Figure 4C), and we subjected mice to surgical removal of iBAT. The serum IL-6 concentration of such mice was not increased after cast immobilization (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from mice with surgically removed iBAT.

claims.claim: The reduction in eWAT mass after cast immobilization in C57BL/6 J mice was suppressed by surgical removal of iBAT.
claims.source: We also found that the reduction in eWAT mass after cast immobilization in C57BL/6 J mice was suppressed by surgical removal of iBAT (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by tissue weight measurements in mice with surgically removed iBAT.

claims.claim: BAT-derived IL-6 induces lipolysis in WAT.
claims.source: These results suggested that BAT-derived IL-6 induces lipolysis in WAT.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the eWAT mass data from iBAT-depleted mice.

claims.claim: The concentrations of BCAAs in soleus were increased after cast immobilization in mice depleted of iBAT.
claims.source: Whereas the serum concentration of IL-6 in mice depleted of iBAT was not affected by cast immobilization (Figure 6G), the concentrations of BCAAs in soleus were increased after cast immobilization in such mice (Figure 6I–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from mice with surgically removed iBAT.

claims.claim: IL-6 secretion in an autocrine or paracrine manner may regulate BCAA metabolism in skeletal muscle independently of IL-6 derived from iBAT.
claims.source: These data thus suggested that IL-6 secretion in an autocrine or paracrine manner may regulate BCAA metabolism in skeletal muscle independently of IL-6 derived from iBAT.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that BCAA increases persist in muscle even when iBAT is removed.

claims.claim: Expression of Il6 was increased in not immobilized fore limb muscles (biceps brachii muscle; BBM) after cast immobilization.
claims.source: We further found that expression of Il6 was also increased in not immobilized fore limb muscles (biceps brachii muscle; BBM) after cast immobilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from non-immobilized muscles.

claims.claim: BCAA concentrations in BBM were increased after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Furthermore, gene expression for the ubiquitin ligases Atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 in BBM was increased during the early phase of cast immobilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E). BCAA concentrations in BBM were also increased after cast immobilization (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data from non-immobilized muscles.

claims.claim: Acute cold exposure increased expression of Il6 only in iBAT and skeletal muscle in mice.
claims.source: Finally, we investigated whether the thermoregulatory system through amino acid metabolism in the interaction between BAT and skeletal muscle also plays an important role in other conditions, such as cold temperature and restraint stress. Acute cold exposure increased expression of Il6 only in iBAT and skeletal muscle in mice (Figure 7A), and expression of Saa3 and Socs3 were increased in soleus (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from cold-exposed mice.

claims.claim: The amounts of valine in soleus were significantly increased by acute cold exposure in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, the amounts of valine in soleus were significantly increased by acute cold exposure in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice (Figure 7B-D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice during cold exposure.

claims.claim: Restraint stress for 6 hr on mice increased expression of Ucp1 in iBAT.
claims.source: Restraint stress for 6 hr on mice increased expression of Ucp1 in iBAT (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), and the amounts of Il6 mRNA was increased in iBAT and skeletal muscle (Figure 7E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from restraint-stressed mice.

claims.claim: BCAA concentrations in soleus were tended to increased by restraint stress in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice.
claims.source: BCAA concentrations in soleus were tended to increased by restraint stress in WT mice but not in IL-6 KO mice (Figure 7G-I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data comparing WT and IL-6 KO mice during restraint stress.

claims.claim: Thermoregulatory system through amino acid metabolism in skeletal muscle and BAT may be activated under cold temperature and acute stress.
claims.source: Together, thermoregulatory system through amino acid metabolism in skeletal muscle and BAT may be activated under cold temperature and acute stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the collective data from cold exposure and restraint stress experiments.

claims.claim: Cast immobilisation leads to a passive loss of skeletal muscle function, resulting in failure to maintain adequate core body temperature in a cold environment.
claims.source: We have shown here that cast immobilisation leads to a passive loss of skeletal muscle function, resulting in failure to maintain adequate core body temperature in a cold environment.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the study.

claims.claim: Cast immobilization activated BAT thermogenesis via the sympathetic nervous system and triggered systemic changes in energy metabolism associated with BAT thermogenesis.
claims.source: Cast immobilization also activated BAT thermogenesis via the sympathetic nervous system and triggered systemic changes in energy metabolism associated with BAT thermogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the denervation experiments and metabolic measurements.

claims.claim: Free BCAAs derived from skeletal muscle serve as substrates for energy metabolism in BAT.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that free BCAAs derived from skeletal muscle serve as substrates for energy metabolism in BAT, and that skeletal muscle–derived IL-6 promotes this provision of BAT with amino acids from muscle.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the metabolomics and tracer uptake data.

claims.claim: Skeletal muscle–derived IL-6 promotes the provision of BAT with amino acids from muscle.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that free BCAAs derived from skeletal muscle serve as substrates for energy metabolism in BAT, and that skeletal muscle–derived IL-6 promotes this provision of BAT with amino acids from muscle.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the IL-6 KO and administration experiments.

claims.claim: Shivering is the major source of heat production in acute cold exposure before a sufficient amount of UCP1 can be recruited in BAT.
claims.source: Shivering is the major source of heat production in acute cold exposure before a sufficient amount of UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1) can be recruited in BAT (Tansey and Johnson, 2015; Rowland et al., 2015a; Golozoubova et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on thermogenesis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Shivering is gradually replaced by UCP1-dependent thermogenesis, and nonshivering thermogenesis is necessary for long-term adaptation to a cold environment.
claims.source: Shivering is gradually replaced by UCP1-dependent thermogenesis, and nonshivering thermogenesis is necessary for long-term adaptation to a cold environment (Rowland et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on thermogenesis adaptation.

claims.claim: Skeletal muscle and BAT thermogenesis can compensate in part each other to maintain core body temperature.
claims.source: Skeletal muscle and BAT thermogenesis can compensate in part each other to maintain core body temperature is widely recognaized (Rowland et al., 2015a; Golozoubova et al., 2001; Janovska et al., 2023; Blondin et al., 2017), and a recent study suggests that suppression of BAT thermogenesis has been found to promote thermogenesis in skeletal muscle (Blondin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature on thermogenesis compensation.

claims.claim: Activation of BAT thermogenesis is associated with increased lipid and glucose catabolism.
claims.source: Activation of BAT thermogenesis is associated with increased lipid and glucose catabolism (Heine et al., 2018; Khedoe et al., 2015; Olsen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on BAT metabolism.

claims.claim: Succinate and BCAAs have been found to support BAT thermogenesis.
claims.source: Succinate and BCAAs have also been found to support BAT thermogenesis, however (Mills et al., 2018; Yoneshiro et al., 2019; Yoneshiro et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on alternative BAT substrates.

claims.claim: IL-6 induces various fever responses, including nonshivering thermogenesis in BAT, by promoting prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis in central vascular endothelial cells.
claims.source: IL-6 induces various fever responses, including nonshivering thermogenesis in BAT, by promoting prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis in central vascular endothelial cells (Chen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on IL-6's role in fever.

claims.claim: IL-6 directly affects energy metabolism in various organs, including skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue.
claims.source: On the other hand, IL-6 directly affects energy metabolism in various organs, including skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue (Serrano et al., 2008; Ellingsgaard et al., 2011; Knudsen et al., 2014; van Hall et al., 2003; Nonogaki et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature on IL-6's metabolic effects.

claims.claim: Approximately 50% of systemic skeletal muscle was immobilized by the cast immobilization procedure.
claims.source: We confirmed that ~50% of systemic skeletal muscle was immobilized (Supplementary file 1A), and that the immobilization induced skeletal muscle atrophy within 3–5 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by muscle weight measurements and supplementary data.

claims.claim: The immobilization induced skeletal muscle atrophy within 3–5 days.
claims.source: We confirmed that ~50% of systemic skeletal muscle was immobilized (Supplementary file 1A), and that the immobilization induced skeletal muscle atrophy within 3–5 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by muscle weight measurements over time.

claims.claim: Systemic locomotor activity was decreased during the dark phase in cast-immobilized mice compared to control mice.
claims.source: Systemic locomotor activity was decreased during the dark phase in cast-immobilized mice compared to control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by locomotor activity monitoring data.

claims.claim: The core body temperature showed a tendency to decrease in cast-immobilized mice compared to control mice under room temperature.
claims.source: Hence, the core body temperature showed a tendency to decrease in cast-immobilized mice compared to control mice under room temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements at room temperature.

claims.claim: Cast immobilization decreased the amounts of metabolites in TCA cycle and suppressed expression of mitochondrial-related genes from the early stage of immobilization.
claims.source: We found that cast immobilization decreased the amounts of metabolites in TCA cycle and suppressed expression of mitochondrial-related genes from the early stage of immobilization, suggesting that metabolic rate is rapidly decreased in immobilized muscle.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics and gene expression data, with inference about metabolic rate.

claims.claim: Expression of the gene for sarcolipin was not increased in muscle after cast immobilization.
claims.source: Our results now show that expression of the gene for sarcolipin, a key regulator of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+- ATPase (SERCA) and an important mediator of muscle nonshivering thermogenesis, was not increased in muscle after cast immobilization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data and established knowledge about sarcolipin's role.

claims.claim: UCP3 gene expression in muscle was transiently increased during the early stage of cast immobilization.
claims.source: In contrast, we have now shown that UCP3 gene expression in muscle was transiently increased during the early stage of cast immobilization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data.

claims.claim: Metabolic thermogenesis in skeletal muscle is crucial for mammals.
claims.source: Our results thus show that metabolic thermogenesis in skeletal muscle is crucial for mammals, and that cast immobilization increases cold intolerance, even in BAT-enriched mammals such as rodents.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing cold intolerance.

claims.claim: BAT thermogenesis was activated via the sympathetic nervous system under room temperature even when skeletal muscle was immobilized.
claims.source: In contrast to skeletal muscle, BAT thermogenesis was activated via the sympathetic nervous system under room temperature even when skeletal muscle was immobilized.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the denervation experiments and gene expression data.

claims.claim: The capacity of the BAT itself was insufficient to maintain stable body temperature during acute cold exposure.
claims.source: A bit surprisingly, the capacity of the BAT itself was insufficient to maintain stable body temperature during acute cold exposure.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that cast-immobilized mice still showed hypothermia despite BAT activation.

claims.claim: Skeletal muscle is a source of free amino acids for BAT thermogenesis or hepatic gluconeogenesis.
claims.source: Our results suggest that skeletal muscle is a source of free amino acids for BAT thermogenesis or hepatic gluconeogenesis.

claims.claim: BAT and skeletal muscle cooperate to maintain body temperature in endotherms.

results.result: Cast immobilization of hind limbs in mice induces cold intolerance independently of muscle mass loss and systemic locomotor activity. Bilateral immobilization (affecting ~50% of skeletal muscle) causes greater hypothermia than unilateral immobilization, and cold intolerance is observed as early as 24 hours post-immobilization before significant muscle atrophy occurs (which develops within 3-5 days).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C5, C72, and C73 provide converging experimental evidence from temperature measurements, muscle weight data, and locomotor activity monitoring. The dose-response relationship (unilateral vs. bilateral immobilization, C5) and temporal dissociation between cold intolerance (24h, C2) and muscle atrophy (3-5 days, C73) strengthen the conclusion that immobilization directly impairs thermogenesis independent of muscle mass loss.

results.result: Cast immobilization suppresses thermogenic gene expression and metabolic activity in skeletal muscle. Immobilized muscle shows decreased TCA cycle metabolites, suppressed mitochondrial gene expression, no increase in sarcolipin expression, and fails to upregulate Ucp1, Ucp2, Ucp3, and Ppargc1a in response to cold exposure, indicating impaired muscle thermogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C76, C77, and C78 collectively demonstrate suppressed muscle thermogenic capacity through multiple complementary measurements (gene expression, metabolomics). The lack of cold-induced upregulation of key thermogenic genes (C3, C4) and decreased metabolic activity (C76) provide strong evidence for impaired muscle thermogenesis.

results.result: Cast immobilization activates BAT thermogenesis via the sympathetic nervous system as a compensatory mechanism. BAT shows increased UCP1 and PGC-1α expression, transiently elevated norepinephrine, and surgical denervation of iBAT prevents UCP1 upregulation and exacerbates hypothermia in cast-immobilized mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 provide strong evidence through denervation experiments (C9, C10), which are the gold standard for demonstrating sympathetic dependence. The convergence of molecular markers (UCP1, PGC-1α), neurotransmitter measurements (norepinephrine), and functional outcomes (body temperature) supports the compensatory BAT activation mechanism.

results.result: Cast immobilization triggers systemic metabolic changes including increased carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism in BAT, upregulation of fatty acid and succinate transporters, increased oxygen consumption and lipid utilization, and mobilization of energy stores (reduced eWAT mass and hepatic glycogen). These changes are dependent on sympathetic innervation of BAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 demonstrate coordinated systemic metabolic responses through metabolomics (C12, C15), gene expression (C14), metabolic measurements (C16), and tissue analysis (C17, C18). The denervation experiments (C13) establish that these changes depend on BAT sympathetic activation, strengthening the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Free amino acids accumulate in immobilized skeletal muscle and are preferentially taken up by BAT and liver rather than muscle. Muscle shows increased protein degradation (Atrogin-1, MuRF-1 upregulation), increased amino acid efflux transporter (SLC43A1), and decreased amino acid uptake transporters and catabolic enzymes. Radiotracer studies confirm increased leucine uptake in BAT, liver, and kidney but not muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C28 provide comprehensive evidence through metabolomics (C19), gene expression profiling of transporters and enzymes (C20-C24), and radiotracer uptake studies (C25). The coordinated changes in muscle (increased efflux, decreased uptake/catabolism) and BAT (increased uptake transporters) support amino acid redistribution. However, the radiotracer data (C25) only shows uptake, not utilization, which is a limitation.

results.result: Cast immobilization induces IL-6 expression in both BAT and skeletal muscle, with BAT showing earlier upregulation (6-10 hours) than muscle. IL-6 expression in BAT is dependent on sympathetic innervation, and serum IL-6 levels increase from 10 hours post-immobilization. IL-6 target genes (Saa3, Socs3) are coordinately upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 demonstrate IL-6 induction through comparative gene expression analysis (C29), temporal profiling (C30), target gene validation (C31), denervation experiments (C32), and serum measurements (C33). The denervation experiment (C32) establishes sympathetic dependence for BAT IL-6 expression, though the mechanism for muscle IL-6 induction remains unclear.

results.result: IL-6 deficiency impairs thermoregulation and alters energy metabolism in cast-immobilized mice. IL-6 KO mice show greater hypothermia during cold exposure, no increase in oxygen consumption, impaired amino acid accumulation in BAT, no increase in leucine uptake in BAT, and no loss of eWAT mass after cast immobilization. BCAAs fail to accumulate in muscle of IL-6 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C44 provide comprehensive phenotypic characterization of IL-6 KO mice through body temperature measurements (C36), metabolic assessments (C37), metabolomics (C38, C39, C44), gene expression (C40), tracer uptake (C41), and tissue weights (C42). The convergence of multiple independent measurements supports IL-6's role in coordinating thermoregulation and metabolism.

results.result: IL-6 administration restores BCAA accumulation in skeletal muscle of cast-immobilized IL-6 KO mice and directly increases BCAAs in cultured myotubes. This demonstrates that muscle-derived IL-6 directly regulates BCAA metabolism in skeletal muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 provide rescue experiments in vivo and in vitro that establish IL-6 sufficiency for BCAA accumulation. The in vitro data (C46) demonstrates direct effects on muscle cells, eliminating indirect systemic effects. However, the mechanism by which IL-6 increases BCAAs (altered synthesis, degradation, or transport) is not determined.

results.result: BAT-derived IL-6 contributes to systemic IL-6 levels and promotes lipolysis in white adipose tissue, but muscle-derived IL-6 acts locally in an autocrine/paracrine manner to regulate BCAA metabolism. Surgical removal of iBAT prevents the increase in serum IL-6 and eWAT loss but does not prevent BCAA accumulation in muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 demonstrate tissue-specific IL-6 functions through surgical ablation experiments. The dissociation between serum IL-6 (abolished by iBAT removal, C49) and muscle BCAA accumulation (preserved, C52) supports distinct endocrine (BAT→WAT) and autocrine/paracrine (muscle→muscle) IL-6 functions. However, the inference about autocrine/paracrine signaling (C53) is indirect.

results.result: The thermoregulatory system involving IL-6-mediated amino acid metabolism between BAT and skeletal muscle is activated not only by cast immobilization but also by acute cold exposure and restraint stress. Non-immobilized muscles also show IL-6 upregulation and BCAA accumulation during cast immobilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 extend the findings to other physiological conditions (cold exposure, stress) and demonstrate that the response is not limited to immobilized muscles. The IL-6 dependence is confirmed in cold exposure (C57) and restraint stress (C59) using IL-6 KO mice. This generalization strengthens the physiological relevance of the findings.

results.result: The study establishes that BAT and skeletal muscle cooperate to maintain body temperature through IL-6-mediated redistribution of BCAAs from muscle to BAT. Cast immobilization causes loss of muscle thermogenic function, triggering compensatory BAT thermogenesis that utilizes muscle-derived BCAAs as fuel, with IL-6 coordinating this inter-organ metabolic cooperation.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C61, C63, C64, C89) integrate the major findings and are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence. However, the direct demonstration that muscle-derived BCAAs are the actual fuel source for BAT thermogenesis would require more sophisticated tracing experiments (e.g., isotope labeling from muscle to BAT oxidation products).

results.result: The manuscript correctly cites established knowledge about thermogenesis mechanisms, including the roles of shivering vs. non-shivering thermogenesis, compensation between muscle and BAT, BAT substrate utilization, and IL-6's effects on metabolism and fever responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These establish the context for the current work and appear to accurately represent prior findings based on the citations provided.

results.result: The manuscript appropriately cites prior work on IL-6's role in muscle atrophy, the absence of early inflammation in cast immobilization, the Piezo1-KLF15 axis regulating IL-6, neural regulation of muscle factors, and associations between IL-6/BCAAs and metabolic disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 cite relevant prior literature to contextualize the findings. The citations appear appropriate for establishing what is known about IL-6 regulation and function in muscle and metabolic disease.

results.result: The authors conclude that metabolic thermogenesis in skeletal muscle is crucial for mammals and that BAT capacity alone is insufficient to maintain stable body temperature during acute cold exposure in cast-immobilized mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C79 and C81 are interpretive conclusions supported by the experimental data showing cold intolerance despite BAT activation. However, the generalization to all mammals (C79) is somewhat overstated given that the study only examined mice, which are BAT-enriched rodents. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the discussion.

results.result: Cast immobilization induces cold intolerance in mice, with reduced core body temperature during cold exposure. This occurs even at 24 hours when muscle mass is preserved, and is attenuated in unilateral versus bilateral immobilization. The effect is independent of systemic locomotor activity and involves suppressed thermogenic gene expression in muscle.
results.evaluation: One reviewer fundamentally challenges the experimental model, stating 'cast immobilization does not work as a (passive) loss of function, instead this procedure produces a dramatic gain of function' and that 'the animal is put under enormous stress.' The reviewer argues the results 'could also be attributed to high stress and decreased calorie reserves' and questions whether conclusions about thermogenesis can be drawn when 'mice are in acute recovery from the anesthetic.' However, another reviewer acknowledges the authors 'thoroughly and comprehensively examined the changes' and finds the organ interaction 'convincingly demonstrated,' though notes 'the impact of immobilization on the function of skeletal muscle and BAT during cold exposure has not been thoroughly analyzed.'

results.result: BAT thermogenesis is activated via the sympathetic nervous system in cast-immobilized mice, with increased UCP1 and PGC-1α expression, elevated norepinephrine, and denervation experiments showing dependence on sympathetic innervation for both gene expression and temperature maintenance.
results.evaluation: One reviewer fundamentally rejects the interpretation, stating 'the BAT is stressed by this procedure, becoming super-induced but relatively poor functioning' and that this represents 'an inaccurate experimental construct' leading to 'wrong conclusions.' The reviewer argues the results reflect 'the resilience and adaptation of mouse physiology in the face of dragging around hind limb casts' rather than organ communication during thermogenic challenge. Another reviewer, however, finds the work demonstrates 'the significance of this organ interaction' convincingly, though with reservations about completeness of analysis during cold exposure.

results.result: Cast immobilization triggers metabolic changes in BAT including increased carbohydrate metabolites, amino acids, and transporter expression (dependent on sympathetic innervation), along with increased oxygen consumption, lipid utilization, and depletion of WAT and hepatic glycogen stores.
results.evaluation: One reviewer challenges the interpretation of these metabolic changes, stating 'within hours and days of CI, there is massive muscle loss...and loss of lipid reserves in adipose and liver. The lipid cycle that maintains BAT thermogenesis is depleted.' The reviewer argues these represent 'cachectic effects on muscle and fat' due to stress rather than adaptive thermogenic responses. The editor notes 'the evidence for the claim is incomplete, as cast immobilization...may impact muscle and BAT directly, and imposes an energetic cost of motion on the animal that is not accounted for.'

results.result: Free amino acids accumulate in immobilized muscle with increased expression of ubiquitin ligases and altered transporter expression. Leucine tracer uptake is increased in BAT, liver, and kidney but not muscle, suggesting amino acids from muscle serve as substrates for BAT thermogenesis and hepatic gluconeogenesis.
results.evaluation: One reviewer interprets these findings as stress-induced catabolism rather than adaptive substrate provision, noting 'massive muscle loss (leading to high circulating BCAAs)' as part of the overall cachectic response. The editor states 'further experiments are also needed to directly assess the role of adipose-derived BCAAs in thermogenesis,' indicating the evidence for the proposed mechanism is incomplete. However, another reviewer acknowledges the authors 'thoroughly and comprehensively examined the changes in skeletal muscle and BAT.'

results.result: IL-6 gene expression is induced earlier and more strongly than other cytokines in both iBAT (6-10 hours) and soleus muscle after cast immobilization. IL-6 expression in iBAT is dependent on sympathetic innervation, and serum IL-6 levels increase from 10 hours post-immobilization.
results.evaluation: One reviewer views IL-6 induction as part of the stress response, stating the procedure induces 'IL6 expression in a variety of tissues, together with commensurate cachectic effects on muscle and fat.' The reviewer notes 'the absence of positive results from your stress assays does not exclude stress as the primary source of the results.' However, another reviewer finds the IL-6 experiments suggest 'this cytokine is likely involved in the supply of amino acids from skeletal muscle to BAT,' indicating some acceptance of the mechanistic role.

results.result: IL-6 knockout mice show impaired thermoregulation during cast immobilization with greater hypothermia during cold exposure, no increase in oxygen consumption, altered metabolite profiles in BAT (higher baseline carbohydrates, no increase in amino acids), reduced leucine uptake in BAT, and no loss of WAT mass. BCAAs fail to increase in muscle of IL-6 KO mice.
results.evaluation: The IL-6 knockout experiments are not specifically criticized by reviewers. One reviewer acknowledges 'the experiments with IL-6 knockout mice and IL-6 administration to these mice suggest that this cytokine is likely involved in the supply of amino acids from skeletal muscle to BAT.' The genetic loss-of-function approach provides stronger evidence than the immobilization model alone, though the overall interpretation remains contested due to concerns about the immobilization paradigm itself.

results.result: IL-6 administration restores BCAA accumulation in muscle of IL-6 KO mice and increases BCAAs in cultured myotubes. IL-6 does not increase body temperature in denervated mice. Surgical removal of iBAT prevents serum IL-6 increase and WAT loss but not muscle BCAA accumulation, suggesting autocrine/paracrine IL-6 regulation in muscle.
results.evaluation: These gain-of-function and tissue-specific manipulation experiments are not directly criticized by reviewers. One reviewer notes the authors 'convincingly demonstrating the significance of this organ interaction' through their comprehensive examination. The iBAT removal experiments provide additional mechanistic insight that helps address the editor's concern about needing 'further experiments...to directly assess' the mechanisms involved.

results.result: The IL-6-mediated amino acid metabolism system is also activated in non-immobilized forelimb muscles during cast immobilization, during acute cold exposure (with IL-6-dependent valine increases in muscle), and during restraint stress (with trends toward IL-6-dependent BCAA increases), suggesting a general thermoregulatory mechanism.
results.evaluation: While these experiments extend the findings to other conditions, one reviewer's fundamental critique of the immobilization model as a stress paradigm applies here as well. The reviewer states the approach 'cannot be interpreted at all in terms of organ communication during thermogenic challenge.' However, the cold exposure experiments may be less confounded than immobilization, and another reviewer specifically notes 'the impact of immobilization on the function of skeletal muscle and BAT during cold exposure has not been thoroughly analyzed,' suggesting this area needs more work rather than being fundamentally flawed.

results.result: The cast immobilization procedure immobilized approximately 50% of systemic skeletal muscle, induced muscle atrophy within 3-5 days, decreased locomotor activity during the dark phase, and caused a tendency toward decreased core body temperature at room temperature.
results.evaluation: One reviewer challenges the characterization of these effects, noting 'CI suppresses 50% locomoter activity, but the actual work done by the mouse carrying bilateral casts is not taken into account (how heavy are they?)' and that 'other muscles in the mouse body are compensating to allow the mouse to drag itself to the food source.' The reviewer questions whether 'the demand for heat even the same when the mouse is wrapped in gypsum,' indicating these baseline characterizations may not support the intended interpretation of passive muscle loss.

results.result: Cast immobilization decreased TCA cycle metabolites and mitochondrial gene expression in muscle, did not increase sarcolipin expression, but transiently increased UCP3. The authors conclude metabolic thermogenesis in skeletal muscle is crucial for mammals and that BAT capacity alone is insufficient to maintain body temperature during acute cold exposure.
results.evaluation: One reviewer fundamentally disputes these conclusions, stating the results 'could also be attributed to high stress and decreased calorie reserves' rather than representing a test of muscle thermogenic capacity. The reviewer argues 'I cannot be convinced that this approach (CI) can be interpreted at all in terms of organ communication during thermogenic challenge.' The editor notes 'the overall approach is innovative but on balance the evidence for the claim is incomplete.'
